image_description:
## 1) Chart type
- **Thematic geographic map** of the United States with **arrow glyphs** plotted by county.

## 2) Layout techniques
- Uses a **map-based spatial layout** (counties positioned by geographic location).
- No faceting or small multiples.
- Not stacked.
- Repeated **glyphs (arrows)** encode county-level values across the map.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| County | Categorical/nominal | One arrow per county; geographic position on the map |
| Geographic location | Spatial | Position on the U.S. map |
| Direction of change in population share | Categorical/nominal | Arrow direction/orientation (up-right vs up-left as shown in legend) |
| Magnitude of percentage-point change in share | Quantitative | Arrow length/size |
| Population group whose share increased (white vs people of color) | Categorical/nominal | Arrow color/hue (red for white, teal for people of color) |
| State name/abbreviation | Categorical/nominal | Text labels |
| City name | Categorical/nominal | Text labels |

Notes visible in the graphic indicate arrows represent **percentage-point change in share** and that counties with changes below one percentage point are not shown.

raw_comment:
I notice that overall from 2010 to 2020 the share of people of color has increased significantly, with the growth experienced overtaking that of the white population by manyfold.  In particular, there has been a lot of growth in the POC population in the midwest and the east. The blue arrows are most concentrated around large cities on the map. Additionally, counties with longer arrows, or more growth, are concentrated around cities also. While growth in POC can be seen across the entire map, that of the white population is limited to a few areas. Mainly, the share of the white population in the southeast. 

To start, I wonder what is prompting the substantial growth in the POC population. Besides the concentration of this growth around large cities, I am intrigued by how evenly this growth is distributed in other parts of the map in the Midwest and the east coast. On the other hand, I wonder why there is far less growth in the western part of the United, especially California which I believe has one of the highest if not the highest minority populations in the U.S.

This relates to me and my community as an Asian American living in a white-dominated area. It is nice to visually see the significant increase in the POC population and process that the areas we live in are becoming more diverse. As the POC population increases, hopefully, that will parallel their representation and inclusion.

What direction has diversity in American been going in the past 10 years?

- **Thematic geographic map** of the United States with **arrow glyphs** plotted by county.

## 2) Layout techniques
- Uses a **map-based spatial layout** (counties positioned by geographic location).
- No faceting or small multiples.
- Not stacked.
- Repeated **glyphs (arrows)** encode county-level values across the map.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| County | Categorical/nominal | One arrow per county; geographic position on the map |

| Direction of change in population share | Categorical/nominal | Arrow direction/orientation (up-right vs up-left as shown in legend) |
| Magnitude of percentage-point change in share | Quantitative | Arrow length/size |
| Population group whose share increased (white vs people of color) | Categorical/nominal | Arrow color/hue (red for white, teal for people of color) |
| State name/abbreviation | Categorical/nominal | Text labels |
| City name | Categorical/nominal | Text labels |

- **Thematic geographic map** of the United States with **arrow glyphs** plotted by county.

- Uses a **map-based spatial layout** (counties positioned by geographic location).
- No faceting or small multiples.
- Not stacked.
- Repeated **glyphs (arrows)** encode county-level values across the map.

|---|---|---|
| County | Categorical/nominal | One arrow per county; geographic position on the map |

| Magnitude of percentage-point change in share | Quantitative | Arrow length/size |
| Population group whose share increased (white vs people of color) | Categorical/nominal | Arrow color/hue (red for white, teal for people of color) |
| State name/abbreviation | Categorical/nominal | Text labels |
| City name | Categorical/nominal | Text labels |

raw_comment: This graph was particularly interesting in the information it revealed. I noticed right away the large prevalence of blue arrows over red ones. In just about every location in the U.S., the share of people of color has increased. This is especially true in the eastern half of the country where the density of blue arrows is greater. Cities like Atlanta and New York City also seem to be filled with blue. The only areas where the share of the white population increased was dotted in places around Texas, South Carolina, Georgia, and a little bit of Louisiana. I wonder what the primary cause of this is. Is it because of immigration? Is it because of a difference in birth rates among different racial populations? Is it because of different groups of people moving across the country to different places? I live in Illinois, one of the places shown to have increasing diversity in the graph as evidenced by the density of arrows. It affects me, because I see a diverse group of people around me in my day to day life. In my opinion, it has caused me to be more aware of the various types of people and cultures that exist. A potential title for this graph, perhaps a bit dramatic but descriptive nonetheless, may be, “America, the melting pot of cultures”.

image_description:
## 1) Chart type
- **Thematic geographic map** of the United States with **arrow glyphs** plotted by county.

## 2) Layout techniques
- Uses a **map-based spatial layout** (counties positioned by geographic location).
- No faceting or small multiples.
- Not stacked.
- Repeated **glyphs (arrows)** encode county-level values across the map.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| County | Categorical/nominal | One arrow per county; geographic position on the map |
| Geographic location | Spatial | Position on the U.S. map |
| Direction of change in population share | Categorical/nominal | Arrow direction/orientation (up-right vs up-left as shown in legend) |
| Magnitude of percentage-point change in share | Quantitative | Arrow length/size |
| Population group whose share increased (white vs people of color) | Categorical/nominal | Arrow color/hue (red for white, teal for people of color) |
| State name/abbreviation | Categorical/nominal | Text labels |
| City name | Categorical/nominal | Text labels |

Notes visible in the graphic indicate arrows represent **percentage-point change in share** and that counties with changes below one percentage point are not shown.
raw_comment: I noticed that from 2010 to 2020, the majority of counties in the United States had an increase in population for people of color, rather than white people. I also noticed that the population increases per county were mainly occurring in the East, and in the West population increases weren't as great. I also saw that there were hardly any population increases in the Southwest like, New Mexico, Arizona, and Nevada. I wonder why the population of people in color increased in the East, but not as much as the West. Is it maybe because there are less jobs/educational programs in the West, or are there more opportunities in the East? I also wonder why the Southwest has a significantly less population increase than any other area in the country. This relates to me because in this map, I live in Illinois and it is right in the middle of the huge population increase zone. I do know that there are a lot of jobs in Illinois especially Chicago, so maybe that is why more people decide to come to areas like Chicago and in the East. My dad works in Chicago, and it is always really busy with businesses and there are many opportunities for incomers. This graph really does show us how there can be almost favorites for where people of color like to live, and I wonder why it is more popular for people of color to choose the East rather than the West. A catchy title for this could be, "Is the West not the best?"

raw_comment: I noticed in this graph that obviously, in a vast majority of places the POC population increased more than the non-hispanic white population did, often significantly so. There was one cluster of tracts in the southeastern coastal states that saw an increase to the contrary, with white growth exceeding that of POC, as well as a few outliers scattered around the country seemingly at random. It makes me wonder as to what could be the cause of that clustering of data in the southeast that went against the trend. Perhaps certain immigration trends there, or simply an existing population makeup that is overwhelmingly white. I’m also curious about what are likely the long term effects of this trend, politically and socially. Mostly, I hypothesize that the change that is occurring and that will likely continue to occur is generally positive. From what this graph shows, in some time the voter bases in most places will be composed of significantly more POC, although obviously some delay from the census is likely. Maybe minorities becoming a somewhat larger component of the population will help speed along social and political reforms for some of society’s race related issues, such as institutional racism in police departments that there has been such a huge movement to fix lately. Certainly even in my own community I can catch a glimpse of some of these issues, and the reform movements that come along with them. “Colored population swell brings hope for future reforms”

image_description:
## 1) Chart type
- **Thematic geographic map** of the United States with **arrow glyphs** plotted by county.

## 2) Layout techniques
- Uses a **map-based spatial layout** (counties positioned by geographic location).
- No faceting or small multiples.
- Not stacked.
- Repeated **glyphs (arrows)** encode county-level values across the map.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| County | Categorical/nominal | One arrow per county; geographic position on the map |
| Geographic location | Spatial | Position on the U.S. map |
| Direction of change in population share | Categorical/nominal | Arrow direction/orientation (up-right vs up-left as shown in legend) |
| Magnitude of percentage-point change in share | Quantitative | Arrow length/size |
| Population group whose share increased (white vs people of color) | Categorical/nominal | Arrow color/hue (red for white, teal for people of color) |
| State name/abbreviation | Categorical/nominal | Text labels |
| City name | Categorical/nominal | Text labels |

Notes visible in the graphic indicate arrows represent **percentage-point change in share** and that counties with changes below one percentage point are not shown.

## 1) Chart type
- **Thematic geographic map** of the United States with **arrow glyphs** plotted by county.

## 2) Layout techniques
- Uses a **map-based spatial layout** (counties positioned by geographic location).
- No faceting or small multiples.
- Not stacked.
- Repeated **glyphs (arrows)** encode county-level values across the map.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| County | Categorical/nominal | One arrow per county; geographic position on the map |
| Geographic location | Spatial | Position on the U.S. map |
| Direction of change in population share | Categorical/nominal | Arrow direction/orientation (up-right vs up-left as shown in legend) |
| Magnitude of percentage-point change in share | Quantitative | Arrow length/size |
| Population group whose share increased (white vs people of color) | Categorical/nominal | Arrow color/hue (red for white, teal for people of color) |
| State name/abbreviation | Categorical/nominal | Text labels |
| City name | Categorical/nominal | Text labels |

Notes visible in the graphic indicate arrows represent **percentage-point change in share** and that counties with changes below one percentage point are not shown.

raw_comment:
As apparently obvious by the sea of green arrows, the American population is becoming generally more diverse. However, some red arrows display that the share of the white population has increased; These red arrows are mostly spread out and oftentimes are due simply to chance. One may notice, though, that The Texas-Mexico border is drastically increasing their white population, and parts of South Carolina & Georgia too. Don’t be mistaken by the graph’s design, there are many smaller counties in the Eastern states compared to the Western states. This could potentially convey a wrong message that the West has barely been supporting diversity because the East is covered in many more green arrows. I also think that the designer’s choice of green being an increase in PoC per capita and red is an increase in white population per capita shows their stance on diversity. 

One of the main outliers in the widespread increase in diversity is the Texas-Mexico border. I wonder why their share of the white population has increased. We should also take into account the Census’ way of measuring these groups, how these definitions changed, and the graph designer’s choice to only measure White vs. PoC changes. Due to the county's proximity to Mexico, it’s interesting that there are more non-Hispanic whites. Perhaps people who have identified as Latino rather than Non-Hispanic white have entered those neighborhoods? (1/2)

raw_comment:
I have noticed that there has been widespread increase in the population of people of color throughout the United States. While there are only a few exceptions in souther/southeastern areas like Georgia, South Carolina, Virginia and Texas. However, there are some interesting outliers, like a tract in Idaho and a tract in Michigan.

I wonder, what is the cause of these outliers? Are they politically, socially, or environmentally based? Furthermore, what is the cause of the 4 tracts across Colorado and New Mexico? What is the reasoning (that is common between two different states) that caused a net increase in the white population in these two tracts?

This relates to my and my community as we can understand where we as a country are headed in terms of acceptance. We are becoming a more nationally diverse country, with people of all races living all across the country.

This graph visualizes the diversification of the United States in a very unique way. A way that on paper you might think would create a very "busy" graph, but really demonstrates how all these little areas can paint an enormous picture when it comes to the nation as a whole. A catchy title for this graph might be "The Wave of Color Washing over the United States"

image_description:
## 1) Chart type
- **Thematic geographic map** of the United States with **arrow glyphs** plotted by county.

## 2) Layout techniques
- Uses a **map-based spatial layout** (counties positioned by geographic location).
- No faceting or small multiples.
- Not stacked.
- Repeated **glyphs (arrows)** encode county-level values across the map.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| County | Categorical/nominal | One arrow per county; geographic position on the map |
| Geographic location | Spatial | Position on the U.S. map |
| Direction of change in population share | Categorical/nominal | Arrow direction/orientation (up-right vs up-left as shown in legend) |
| Magnitude of percentage-point change in share | Quantitative | Arrow length/size |
| Population group whose share increased (white vs people of color) | Categorical/nominal | Arrow color/hue (red for white, teal for people of color) |
| State name/abbreviation | Categorical/nominal | Text labels |
| City name | Categorical/nominal | Text labels |

Notes visible in the graphic indicate arrows represent **percentage-point change in share** and that counties with changes below one percentage point are not shown.

I noticed most places in the United States had an increased share of people of color. The majority of the places that had an increased share of white people was in the South. States like Virginia, North Carolina, South Carolina, Georgia, and other southern states all had a portion that increased the shard of white people. I also noticed the arrow density was much more clustered in the East side of the country, in the Midwest and New England. This means that that area has changed much more in diversity than places in the west like Wyoming. 

I wonder why this change is happening, what are the causes to this change that seems fairly steady across the whole country. I wonder what the explanation is for this fairly universal increase in share of colored people.

## 1) Chart type
- **Thematic geographic map** of the United States with **arrow glyphs** plotted by county.

## 2) Layout techniques
- Uses a **map-based spatial layout** (counties positioned by geographic location).

- Not stacked.

|---|---|---|
| County | Categorical/nominal | One arrow per county; geographic position on the map |

| Population group whose share increased (white vs people of color) | Categorical/nominal | Arrow color/hue (red for white, teal for people of color) |
| State name/abbreviation | Categorical/nominal | Text labels |
| City name | Categorical/nominal | Text labels |

raw_comment: Something I notice that the diversity of the east side of the United States has a far greater increase than the west side, and that there are large growths in northern Georgia, Maryland and New Jersey as well. image_description:
## 1) Chart type
- **Thematic geographic map** of the United States with **arrow glyphs** plotted by county.

## 2) Layout techniques
- Uses a **map-based spatial layout** (counties positioned by geographic location).
- No faceting or small multiples.
- Not stacked.
- Repeated **glyphs (arrows)** encode county-level values across the map.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| County | Categorical/nominal | One arrow per county; geographic position on the map |
| Geographic location | Spatial | Position on the U.S. map |
| Direction of change in population share | Categorical/nominal | Arrow direction/orientation (up-right vs up-left as shown in legend) |
| Magnitude of percentage-point change in share | Quantitative | Arrow length/size |
| Population group whose share increased (white vs people of color) | Categorical/nominal | Arrow color/hue (red for white, teal for people of color) |
| State name/abbreviation | Categorical/nominal | Text labels |
| City name | Categorical/nominal | Text labels |

Notes visible in the graphic indicate arrows represent **percentage-point change in share** and that counties with changes below one percentage point are not shown.

raw_comment:
1. I notice that the population of people of color has largely increased throughout a majority of the U.S. since 2010. This increase happens to be more prevalent on the eastern side of the U.S., while the western side still has increases, but much less.

2. I wonder why the POC population increases in some states more than others. I'd assume it was due to the overall diversity of a state's population, but on the other hand, a state like Arkansas with predominantly white towns that are known to be extremely racist and hateful towards the BIPOC community have still experienced increases in people of color. I guess this would unfortunately lead to even more discrimination and hate toward BIPOC and other people of color.

3. Although the number of people of color in the U.S. has signifcantly increased over time (and still continues to increase), we still experience increasing rates of racism and discrimination. Specifically the BIPOC community experiences a disproportionate amount of racism, despite the diversifying population. I am disgusted by the amount of racism and hate that is still prevalent in society, and will continue to emphasize the importance of advocating for change and social justice.

4. A Decade of Diversity in the U.S. – from 2010 to 2020

This map compares the white and people of color populations from the 2010 and the 2020 U.S. Census.  Each arrow shows the percentage change by county with a change of more than 1 percent.  Note that for this map white is defined as non-Hispanic white. 

From 9 am – 2 pm E.T. today, share with us your responses online to these three questions -- "What do you notice?",  "What do you wonder?"  and “How will this affect you and your community?”  Plus, please share with us a catchy headline that captures the ideas in this graph.

image_description:
## 1) Chart type
- **Thematic geographic map** of the United States with **arrow glyphs** plotted by county.

## 2) Layout techniques
- Uses a **map-based spatial layout** (counties positioned by geographic location).
- No faceting or small multiples.
- Not stacked.
- Repeated **glyphs (arrows)** encode county-level values across the map.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| County | Categorical/nominal | One arrow per county; geographic position on the map |
| Geographic location | Spatial | Position on the U.S. map |
| Direction of change in population share | Categorical/nominal | Arrow direction/orientation (up-right vs up-left as shown in legend) |
| Magnitude of percentage-point change in share | Quantitative | Arrow length/size |
| Population group whose share increased (white vs people of color) | Categorical/nominal | Arrow color/hue (red for white, teal for people of color) |
| State name/abbreviation | Categorical/nominal | Text labels |
| City name | Categorical/nominal | Text labels |

Notes visible in the graphic indicate arrows represent **percentage-point change in share** and that counties with changes below one percentage point are not shown.
raw_comment:
Diversity Shifts in POC Populations in the U.S. over the Last Decade 

Right off the bat, I'm noticing that populations of people of color have crowded around the East Coast, the SouthEast, as well as Midwest. This implies that the populations of POC (people of color) have definitely increased; in other words, diversity throughout the U.S. has gone up. I find it interesting that changes in white populations on the other hand have stayed relatively the same in comparison. This makes me wonder about the different factors that may have influenced non-white communities to expand away from the western states. I also think it is interesting that states like Georgia, that have historically been largely populated with people of color, has started to see an equally amount of increases in white communities. I'm also thinking if there will be any negative impacts in the long run with more people crowding into a specific area of the U.S. (e.g. overpopulation in cities). 

These changes in diversity relates to my community when considering how the area I live in is populated with a large white population. The significant changes in diversity through out the East Coast makes me wonder how the population might change in my area in the next decade.
